meta.description: Yes, this one is really John Muir. It comes from his 1877 essay “Mormon Lilies” — and his sentence actually begins with “But.”

meta.ogDescription: Genuinely John Muir, from his essay “Mormon Lilies” (1877; collected in Steep Trails, 1918). The popular version quietly drops his opening “But.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1838–1914 · Scottish-American naturalist & “Father of the National Parks”
answer.sourceLine: This is genuine Muir. The line appears in his essay “Mormon Lilies,” first published in the San Francisco Daily Evening Bulletin on 19 July 1877 and later collected as Chapter 9 of Steep Trails ↗ (1918). Muir’s own sentence opens with a word the popular version drops: “But in every walk with Nature one receives far more than he seeks.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: San Francisco Daily Evening Bulletin, 19 July 1877, p. 4

source.excerpt: But in every walk with Nature one receives far more than he seeks. I had not gone more than a mile from Lake Point ere I found the way profusely decked with flowers, mostly compositae and purple leguminosae, a hundred corollas or more to the square yard…
trail: The exact sentence appears in the primary text of “Mormon Lilies,” Chapter 9 of Steep Trails ↗, hosted in full by the Sierra Club.
The U.S. National Park Service John Muir quotes page ↗ lists the line in its fuller form — “But in every walk with Nature one receives far more than he seeks” — and credits Steep Trails.
The University of the Pacific’s John Muir bibliography ↗ records the essay’s original run in the San Francisco Daily Evening Bulletin, 19 July 1877.
source.excerptNote: The sentence opens the paragraph in which Muir describes climbing from Lake Point on the Great Salt Lake up through miles of wildflowers toward the snow.

source.rightsNote: Muir’s essay was first published in 1877 and collected in Steep Trails in 1918; both dates are well before 1931, so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: John Muir
author.heading: About John Muir
author.bio: John Muir was a Scottish-born American naturalist whose books and essays helped launch the modern conservation movement and earned him the nickname the “Father of the National Parks.” He co-founded the Sierra Club in 1892 and campaigned for the protection of Yosemite and other wild lands. His rapturous prose about mountains, forests, and glaciers — much of it drawn from his own long solitary walks — is the natural home for a line like this one.

misattribution.heading: A note on the wording
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare feel-good nature lines pinned on a famous name that turns out to be genuinely his. The catch is smaller: the popular version quietly trims Muir’s actual sentence.

items.why: Muir wrote “But in every walk with Nature one receives far more than he seeks,” with a capital “Nature.” The widely shared version drops the opening “But” and lowercases “nature,” as seen against the primary text ↗.
Quote sites usually stop at the 1918 book. The sentence is older: it first appeared in Muir’s newspaper essay “Mormon Lilies” in 1877, per the University of the Pacific bibliography ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution to John Muir is correct — the line is his, from “Mormon Lilies” (1877; collected in Steep Trails, 1918 ↗). Just remember his sentence starts with “But.”

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Muir wrote the line not as a standalone aphorism but as the opening of a naturalist’s report. Climbing from the shore of the Great Salt Lake toward the snow line, he found the trail “profusely decked with flowers” — the “far more” he received was a hillside of blooms he had not gone looking for.
That grounding is part of why the quote endures: it distills a lifetime of Muir’s solitary walking into a single promise about paying attention to the wild.
